Four years ago I joined Partnership for the Future, Inc. (PFF) as a high school student with a lot of ambition and not much else. Today I walked across the stage and became a collegiate member of Partnership for the Future. Reaching for the Stars was the final act of my Level 4 year, and it meant exactly what it sounds like. It was the moment our class officially closed the high school chapter and stepped into PFF's collegiate program. Names called one by one. College announced. Scholarships earned read out loud for the room to hear. Then came the individual awards: each one tied to values PFF has spent years pushing us to embody. Here's what I walked away with: • Earned the American Corporate Growth Scholarship ($1,000) • Earned PFF's Shooting Star Scholarship ($1,000) • Was nominated for PFF's prestigious Kirshner Scholarship Award But the number that hits different: my class of 2026 earned a combined $25,603,436 in scholarships. The most in PFF history. I'm proud to have been part of that. Four years of this program gave me more than skills. It gave me a community to come back to. It gave me the courage to step outside my comfort zone. It gave me a reason to keep pushing forward. And it gave me the professional resources to build a brand I'm genuinely proud of. Someone once told me you grow the most when you're surrounded by people who push you to be more than you thought you could be. Couldn't be more proud to call PFF my people.

This summer, I had the opportunity to work at CarMax as a Technology intern, focused on building AI-powered tools to help engineering teams automatically monitor and troubleshoot production systems. Our work centered on designing agentic AI workflows that could reason over internal codebases and cloud infrastructure to investigate system issues and identify root causes. Through this project, I gained hands-on experience with agent orchestration, cloud infrastructure, and building reliable, production-grade AI systems. One of the most rewarding parts of this project was seeing how thoughtful engineering can directly reduce the manual burden on a team, turning what used to take hours of investigation into something automated and consistent. This summer also taught me a lot about teamwork and collaboration. Working closely with my team showed me how much stronger a solution becomes when it's shaped by different perspectives, whether that meant talking through a tricky design decision, giving and receiving feedback on code, or just checking in with each other when something wasn't working. I also loved getting to know the other interns, from working through problems together to just hanging out outside of work, and I'm thankful for the friendships and shared experiences we built along the way. I'm incredibly grateful to have been mentored by Todd Hatton and Robert Brown , and to have worked alongside Kevin Benoy as a teammate. Their guidance and collaboration helped me grow as both an engineer and a teammate. Looking forward to taking these skills with me into future projects! #CarMax #SoftwareEngineering #ArtificialIntelligence

This past weekend, I had the opportunity to attend Y Combinator Startup School 2026, and it reminded me why I love building. One of the biggest highlights was meeting so many innovators. Hearing ambitious ideas discussed with so much passion was easily the highlight of the trip. Shoutout to Ahmed Khaleel , Kunal Pai , Mitchell Sabbadini , Yusuf Afifi , Affaan Mustafa , Syed Rayyan Ali, Rushil Kartik Maniar , and many more awesome builders I had the privilege of meeting this weekend. I was also thrilled to finally connect in-person with students from Duke University who are creating incredible things. Shoutout to: Eric Cai , James Mu , William Vo , Yash Dagade , Arnav Gupta , and all the other talented people I finally got to meet in person. Outside of Startup School, I had the chance to visit Google's San Francisco Office, meet Heba Alazzeh , and attend events including the Exa and PostHog afterparties, where I met more incredible people! Some of the most valuable moments came from conversations with founders, researchers, and engineers who are tackling ambitious problems across AI and beyond. The talks were equally inspiring. Hearing perspectives from Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Boris Cherny, Jeff Dean, and Patrick Collison reinforced just how much opportunity there is to build meaningful technology. More than anything, this weekend reignited my excitement for startups. Being surrounded by people who are constantly learning, experimenting, and solving hard problems is something special. I also realized how incredible the atmosphere is in San Francisco. There is an energy that is hard to describe until you experience it. Everywhere you go, people are chasing ambitious ideas and challenging each other to think bigger. Looking forward to coming back. Now it's time to turn inspiration into execution.

Introducing RETINA from Synapse Semiconductor Our semiconductor lab redesigned the camera pixel to run a cnn layer using stored charges in the pixel to perform matrix matrix multiplications. Its time to rethink how machines see the world. (YC S26)

Synapse Semiconductor (YC S26) is a frontier semiconductor research lab building senses for physical AI. Led by Sanjeev Chauhan and Duke ECE Faculty Tania Roy , Synapse Semiconductor builds image sensors that process AI on the sensor itself. Each pixel captures light and runs neural network computation on the same device, eliminating the need for a GPU while reducing power and latency in edge vision. Today, with the launch of RETINA, they are reimagining the core technology for self-driving cars, drones, and humanoid robotics. Like the New World once was, space is the next great frontier to explore. In the future, drones will navigate using vision alone, robots will scout the Moon for the next colony, and satellites will perceive their environment and react in real time. At the foundation of it all will be Synapse Semiconductor. Congrats on the launch, Sanjeev and Tania! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gDkBEwkp

I started Atlia (YC S26) with one of my closest friends Edmond Niu , and I'm happy to announce today that we have joined Y Combinator . We’ve seen firsthand how hard it is for overextended teams to give every guest a personal, six-star stay. At the same time, high management fees eat into owners’ returns. We’re building Atlia so owners can earn more and every guest feels genuinely cared for. Thanks to Jared Friedman and YC for taking a bet on us, and for all our friends, family and professors for helping us get to where we are. We’re launching next week, and we can’t wait to show what is possible in a traditional industry with today’s technology.
